name: Juanda International Airport
before:
Indonesia's third busiest airport after Jakarta and Bali, about 12 km from central Surabaya in Sedati District. It is the hub for Batik Air and Citilink, a focus city for Garuda Indonesia and an operating base for Lion Air and Super Air Jet.

One unusual thing about it: the land belongs entirely to the Indonesian Navy, and the passenger terminal is a civil enclave inside a naval air station. The airport shares its facilities with the Navy's Naval Aviation Center and with an air force base, so military movements are routine.

Terminal 1 opened in November 2006 and covers 51,500 square metres across three floors with eleven jet bridges. It was funded partly by a Japanese loan, and its roof design takes its shape from the traditional high hat roofs of Sumba.

In 2019 the airport was handling around 500 aircraft a day.

It is named after Djuanda Kartawidjaja, the last Prime Minister of Indonesia, who proposed building it.
after:
Surabaya's airport, about 20 km south of the city in Sedati District, Sidoarjo Regency. Batik Air, Citilink, Garuda Indonesia, Lion Air and Super Air Jet all fly from here.

One unusual thing about it: the land belongs to the Indonesian Navy, and the airport is also a naval air base, so military movements are routine.

Terminal 1 opened in November 2006, paid for partly by a Japanese loan. International flights use Terminal 2, a separate terminal that opened in 2014, so check which one a client needs.

It is named after Djuanda Kartawidjaja, whom President Sukarno sent to rescue its construction from a financial crisis.

The hub, focus-city and base labels rest on Wikipedia alone (no airline page naming Surabaya as a hub was reached), so the text now says only that all five fly from here. Antara (19 March 2026) quotes the airport's general manager naming all five on the Surabaya to Bali flights stopped for Nyepi; the regulator's route list for Juanda has all five. InJourney's September 2026 release also names Lion Air and Citilink adding flights at Juanda, and Antara (12 February 2026) Lion Air and Garuda Indonesia operating its umrah flights in 2025.

claims.claim: named after Djuanda Kartawidjaja, whom President Sukarno sent to rescue its construction from a financial crisis
claims.inAfter: It is named after Djuanda Kartawidjaja, whom President Sukarno sent to rescue its construction from a financial crisis.
claims.note: Was 'the last Prime Minister of Indonesia, who proposed building it'. Both detailed accounts say that when the French contractor threatened to pull out over money, Sukarno gave Djuanda a mandate to resolve the crisis and see the project finished, and the base was named after him for that; neither says he proposed it (Liputan6 dates the idea to the Navy's aviation bureau, founded in 1956). Only Wikipedia's lead says he proposed it. Liputan6 draws on the book Surabaya Punya Cerita.

claims.claim: Indonesia's third busiest airport after Jakarta and Bali
claims.wasBefore: Indonesia's third busiest airport after Jakarta and Bali
claims.why: No national ranking dated within 12 months could be read. Airport Technology's 'third busiest' is for 2011. Statistics Indonesia (bps.go.id) refused both a plain request and the browser (403); the regulator's yearly air transport statistics are released only through a request form, and its 2019 book is seven years old; InJourney's annual report page offers no file. The regulator's own Juanda page gives 7,427,121 passengers for 2025, about half the 14,033,162 that Wikipedia takes from the same regulator for 2024, so the page's count is not a full-year total and was not used to rank. Wikipedia alone is not enough.
